claims.text: Premelting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale chemical heterogeneities.
Surface chemical heterogeneities generate spatially variable local cohesive energies.
Regions containing enriched atomic clusters undergo premelting transitions earlier than other regions.
The nanoparticles are initially solid.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu distribution is nominally homogeneous.
The initial elemental distribution contains statistical compositional fluctuations.
Slow heating in vacuum or inert gas promotes equilibrium thermal behavior and minimizes oxidation.
For particles larger than approximately 30 nm, high surface-to-volume effects dominate while extreme size effects are avoided.
Variations in local atomic arrangements produce heterogeneous interfacial energies in the HEA nanoparticles.
Locally enriched species or atomic clusters have weaker cohesive forces.
Reduced local cohesive forces lower the local melting temperature.
Lower local melting temperatures trigger premature surface melting.
Single-metal nanoparticles melt more uniformly than the proposed HEA nanoparticles.
Premelting will initiate non-uniformly at surface regions associated with atomic clusters or compositional fluctuations.
The HEA nanoparticles will display spatially heterogeneous melting features relative to single-metal or simpler-alloy baselines.
Ag and Au nanoparticles, and well-mixed binary-alloy nanoparticles, exhibit uniform melting because cohesive energies are consistent across each particle.
The proposed mechanism applies to multielement HEA nanoparticles whose constituent elements have comparable atomic sizes and mixing enthalpies.
Particles much smaller than 30 nm may fall outside the regime in which chemical heterogeneities govern melting.
Very rapid heating may move the particles outside the regime in which chemical heterogeneities govern melting.
Uniform melting with no correlation between local composition and premelting onset would falsify the proposed heterogeneity-controlled mechanism.
